summary: Defines Per-Domain Behaviors for Differentiated Services and sets out the format and procedure for proposing new ones to the working group. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A whole network can promise how it treats certain traffic. This sets rules for describing those promises.

questions: what is a diffserv per domain behavior
what is a per domain behavior
what is the best effort pdb
subtitle: Defines the Per-Domain Behavior: what a whole diffserv network promises a group of packets, edge to edge, plus the template for describing one.

tldr.problem: Differentiated services defined how each router treats packets (per-hop behaviors), but not how to describe the treatment a group of packets gets across a whole domain from entry to exit.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3086 defines the Per-Domain Behavior (PDB): a classifier, traffic conditioning at the edge and a PHB inside the domain, described by measurable attributes. It also sets a mandatory format and review procedure for proposing new PDBs.
tldr.outcome: It gives a shared vocabulary and a specification template, with Best Effort as the one reference PDB. It is Informational and is not obsoleted.

today: RFC 3086 is an Informational RFC, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the Per-Domain Behavior term and the specification format it describes. It builds on RFC 2474 and RFC 2475.

sections.title: Why Per-Domain Behaviors
sections.content:
Differentiated Services (diffserv) already had per-hop behaviors (PHBs), which describe how a single router treats packets that carry a given codepoint. The diffserv working group (WG) wanted the next step: describing what happens to a group of packets as they cross an entire DS domain, from the ingress edge to the egress edge.

RFC 3086 calls this the Per-Domain Behavior (PDB): the expected treatment that an identifiable or target group of packets receives from edge to edge of a DS domain. A particular PHB (or list of PHBs) and traffic conditioning requirements are associated with each PDB.

The RFC is careful to separate a PDB from a service. A PDB is a technical building block for configuring a domain. Providers are not expected to expose it to customers, and the measurable parameters of a PDB are only expected to be among those cited, directly or indirectly, in a Service Level Specification.
sections.eli5: A single traffic cop decides what happens to one car. A PDB describes what happens to a whole convoy of cars driving through the entire city.

sections.title: Traffic Aggregates and the Two Parts of a PDB
sections.content:
The RFC adds one definition to the ones from RFC 2474 and RFC 2475: a traffic aggregate is a collection of packets with a codepoint that maps to the same PHB, usually in a DS domain or some subset of one. It generalizes the older idea of a behavior aggregate from a single link to a network.

A PDB acts on a target group of packets that a classifier picks out at the domain edge (the classifier may be null). The effect has two parts:

  • Crossing the edge: traffic conditioning (marking, shaping, policing) turns the target group into a traffic aggregate, and conforming packets are marked with the DSCP for the PDB's PHB. Any loss here is controlled by the upstream sender conforming to the traffic conditioning.
  • Crossing the domain: the transit treatment the aggregate gets between any two edges of the domain boundary. The DSCP should not change in the interior; if remarking is needed, there should be a DS boundary at that point.

A PDB must hold as aggregates split and merge inside the domain. A PDB definition does not have to hold for arbitrary topologies, but the limits of its applicability must be clearly stated.
sections.eli5: At the front door, a guard checks who is in the group and sorts them into a line. Inside, everyone in that line is treated the same way all the way to the back door.

sections.title: Constructing PDBs from PHBs
sections.content:
Characterizing a PDB means understanding what a PHB does under aggregation, because PHBs applied recursively across merging and diverging traffic must still give a known behavior. For example, maximum burst sizes grow with the number of microflows merged, and a PDB specification must address this.

Multiple PDBs may use the same PHB. A PDB specification may list several PHBs that all give the same PDB, but a single domain is expected to use a single PHB for a given PDB. PDBs that share a PHB have the same transit performance, though they may claim different attributes.

PHB groups can be used in several ways. One PDB can use a single member of a group such as a Class Selector PHB, or several members of the same group such as the three AF1x PHBs. A set of related PDBs built on a PHB group should be defined in the same document, with each PDB's transit attributes in its own subsection.

PHBs, classifiers and traffic conditioners sit in the forwarding path at line rates. Control plane changes to them are not expected per packet, and the time scale of those changes should not affect the PDB's attributes.
sections.eli5: You can build the same kind of convoy rule from different road rules. What matters is that the convoy gets the same treatment when it splits up and joins other traffic.

sections.title: How a PDB Specification Is Written
sections.content:
Every PDB specification must contain these sections, though their length and content will vary:

  • Applicability Statement: the intended use and the limits to its use.
  • Technical specification: the classification, traffic conditioning and PHBs required, with the rules marked as may, must and should.
  • Attributes: how the PDB behaves under ideal conditions if configured as specified, such as drop rate, throughput or delay bounds. They must be explicit, quantifiable and defensible, and the document must say how statistics were measured and derived.
  • Parameters: network-specific features the PDB depends on, such as maximum number of hops or minimum bandwidth.
  • Assumptions: usually lossless links, no link failures and relatively stable routing, which must be stated.
  • Example uses: short motivating examples.
  • Environmental concerns: constraints on topology or media.
  • Security considerations specific to the PDB.

Section 6 adds guidance on attributes. It separates long-term average behavior (rates or throughput over a stated period) from short-term behavior (how large a burst can be and how many packets can queue at once), and walks through a ring-shaped domain to show how topology changes and bursts can break assumed bounds.
sections.eli5: It is a form every new PDB has to fill in: what it is for, what it promises, what it needs, and what could go wrong.

sections.title: The Reference Best Effort PDB
sections.content:
As a reference, the RFC defines a Best Effort (BE) PDB for normal Internet traffic, preserving the pre-diffserv delivery expectation. There are no restrictions on rate and burst beyond the ingress link. The network edge marks packets for the Default PHB from RFC 2474, no other traffic conditioning is required, and interior nodes apply the Default PHB.

Its attribute is summed up as "as much as possible as soon as possible". Packets are not completely starved and may use resources no other aggregate needs. It has no parameters, assumes a properly functioning network, and the RFC lists no specific security exposures for it.
sections.eli5: Best Effort is the plain lane: no special treatment, but you are not shut out, and you can use any space nobody else needs.

sections.title: Getting a PDB Accepted
sections.content:
The guidelines say a PDB draft should follow the format, be submitted as an Internet Draft with "diffserv" in its name, and include deployment experience or convincing simulation results. Discussion should focus first on the merits of the PDB.

With an active diffserv WG, a draft with consensus goes to a review panel set up by the WG co-chairs, expected to take 4 to 8 weeks, then to WG last call, and then to the Area Directors for publication as an Informational RFC in the "PDB series". With no active WG, the authors seek IESG Expert Review as defined in RFC 2434.

The general security considerations of RFC 2474 and RFC 2475 apply to all PDBs, and individual PDBs may need more.
sections.eli5: New PDBs must show they work for real, get checked by a review team, and only then get published.
